clue.text: See 7
Shelter from heat starting with shady area in garden

parts.note: H is the standard abbreviation for heat, placed at the start
a leafy bower or trellised nook giving shade in a garden

explanation.surface: Someone escapes the summer sun by finding a cool shady corner of the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: H plus ARBOUR gives HARBOUR; 'starting' simply puts the heat first.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbour is a place of refuge, and as a verb or noun it means safe cover or protection.

clue.text: Setter's in bed in Paris? This is the end!

indicators.note: the setter's contraction is placed inside the French word for bed

parts.note: lit is French for bed
the setter is 'I', so 'setter's' is read as 'I am', contracted

explanation.surface: A setter lounging in a Parisian bed exclaims that things have gone too far.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags 'in Paris' as meaning 'in French'; the setter's contraction is the first-person 'I am'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'this is the limit!' expresses exasperation that nothing worse can be tolerated, the very end.

clue.text: Liberate dentures for nothing

parts.note: a set of false teeth
costing nothing

explanation.surface: An offer to hand out false teeth without charge.
explanation.definitionFit: To set someone free is to release them from captivity, the same as liberating them.

clue.text: Tremble with terror, but don't say where we got the milk

parts.note: the hushing sound telling someone to keep quiet
the cow's milk-producing gland

explanation.surface: A frightened child is told to keep quiet about where the milk really comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: To shudder is to shake involuntarily, typically from fear or horror.

clue.text: Move fast and maybe illegally to deceive sleuth

indicators.note: acting outside the rules suggests letters not kept in their lawful order

parts.note: a detective, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A con artist rushes about, perhaps breaking the law, to fool a detective on their trail.
explanation.walkthrough: The word has two senses here, hurrying and swindling, both covered by the clue around the rearranged detective.
explanation.definitionFit: To hustle is both to hurry along briskly and, in slang, to con or swindle someone.

clue.text: (and 12,25,1,17,23) Hold high statesman 'til directly at death's door: this will provide his (Pam's) exit line

definitions.text: Hold high statesman 'til directly at death's door: this will provide his (Pam's) exit line

parts.words: Hold high statesman 'til directly at death's door: this will provide his (Pam's) exit line
parts.note: Pam was the nickname of Lord Palmerston, the Victorian prime minister, whose reputed dying words are the answer: a quip about dying being the final act

explanation.surface: A tribute to a great politician, kept upright to the very end, followed by a note on his famous last words.
explanation.walkthrough: The full answer runs over six lights: DIE, MY DEAR DOCTOR, THAT'S THE LAST THING I SHALL DO. Palmerston (Pam) is said to have spoken it to his physician on his deathbed in 1865.
explanation.definitionFit: An exit line is the last remark before leaving, and this was Palmerston's final witty remark before death.

clue.text: Author of 28 19, isn't it? Setter's often got stupid following

definitions.note: cryptic: the word followed by 'stupid' in the slogan

parts.note: Umberto Eco wrote The Name of the Rose
a tag question, like Italian 'no?' at the end of a remark
belonging to the setter, who is 'me'

explanation.surface: A query about a novelist, then a jibe that the setter is often called stupid.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to Clinton's 1992 slogan 'It's the economy, stupid', where the word was always followed by 'stupid'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the famous campaign catchphrase this word was repeatedly followed by the insult, a cryptic allusion rather than a dictionary synonym.

clue.text: Loud German work by German-American psychologist has point: 1 17 23!

definitions.note: cross-reference to THE LAST THING I SHALL DO

parts.note: f, forte, is the musical marking for loud
the German word for work
Erich Fromm, German-born psychoanalyst who worked in America
east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A rather academic note on a German psychologist's work, ending with an emphatic refusal.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'far be it from me' disclaims any intention of doing something, just as 'the last thing I shall do' does.

clue.text: 28 19, the proper one?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: 28 19 reads 'the name of the rose', and the rose called the primrose has ... in front of ROSE as its name
second meaning: a ... person is the stiffly proper one, correct in manners

explanation.walkthrough: 28 19 is THE NAME OF THE ROSE, Umberto Eco's novel, but here it is read literally: the extra word in front of 'rose' in primrose.
explanation.definitionFit: Prim describes someone stiffly correct and formal in manner, the very picture of propriety.

clue.text: One who parts with property legally strikes fans with terror

definitions.text: One who parts with property legally

indicators.note: a blow knocks things about, so the following letters are jolted out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lawyer's client giving up property frightens the onlookers.
explanation.definitionFit: In law a transferor is the party who conveys property or rights to another person.

clue.text: See 7
Left youth hostel initially to be eaten by bear, making a lot of fuss

indicators.note: what is eaten ends up inside the eater

parts.note: Baloo, the bear in Kipling's Jungle Book
L is the usual abbreviation for left

indicators.note: only the opening letter of each word of the lodging is wanted

parts.note: first letters of each word

explanation.surface: A grim tale of a guest leaving a hostel and being devoured by a bear, causing commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: The bear is Baloo from Kipling's The Jungle Book; the two pieces sit after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballyhoo is noisy publicity or commotion, a great to-do about something.

clue.text: Support with backing — quote opening of Hamlet — such was his soul

parts.note: a prop holds something up

indicators.note: going backwards means the quoting word and the opening letter are read right to left

parts.note: to cite is to quote

indicators.note: the opening of anything is its start, so only the first letter of the play is kept

parts.note: first letter of the play's name

explanation.surface: A note on staging Hamlet, propped up from behind, with a nod to the prince's inner life.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet cries 'O my prophetic soul!' on learning his uncle murdered his father, so the definition is a quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet calls his own soul prophetic because it had foreseen the truth about his father's murder.

clue.text: God with love in his finger, age six according to Jacques

parts.note: Pan, Greek god of the wild

indicators.note: the zero-score letter is put inside the god's claw

parts.note: a claw, a bird's finger
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A mythological god with something lodged in his finger, filtered through a Shakespeare speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques's Seven Ages of Man speech in As You Like It makes the sixth age 'the lean and slipper'd pantaloon', a doddering old man.
explanation.definitionFit: In Jaques's Seven Ages speech the sixth age is the old man, the lean and slippered pantaloon.

clue.text: Note instrument turning to stone

parts.note: B is a note of the musical scale

indicators.note: something that turns round faces the other way, so the instrument is read backwards

parts.note: a stringed instrument of ancient Greece

explanation.surface: A musical note played on an instrument that magically turns to stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Beryl is a gemstone mineral, of which emerald and aquamarine are varieties.

clue.text: See 7
As high as his hopes go, the drug will get in there

indicators.note: the answer is said to be found inside the phrase before it

parts.note: the letters run across these words

explanation.surface: A user's hopes rise as high as the drug can take them.
explanation.walkthrough: The words 'As' and 'go' are surface padding: the answer spans the end of high, all of as and his, and the start of hopes.
explanation.definitionFit: Hashish is cannabis resin, a drug commonly smoked to get high.

clue.text: See 28
Author of 28 19 in English river junction

parts.note: the Humber, an English estuary and river in Yorkshire
a T-junction, shaped like the letter

explanation.surface: Pointing out where an English river meets another, with a literary detour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'English' does double duty in the surface; the definition is Umberto Eco's first name put into its English form.
explanation.definitionFit: Umberto, the Italian forename of the novelist Eco, corresponds to the English name Humbert.

clue.text: Phantom's regard inverted

indicators.note: turned upside down so the top part goes to the bottom and the tail comes first

parts.note: to regard highly is to respect

explanation.surface: A ghost is spoken of with awe and upside-down regard.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening two letters move to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectre is a ghost or apparition, the same as a phantom.

clue.text: Warning, spirit style

parts.note: a la, in the style of
rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: A list of three nouns, like a heading for a cocktail menu.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the reverse of clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Alarum is the archaic form of alarm, a call to arms or warning of danger.

clue.text: See 7
See 27
See 7
Weight of timber to crash violently into…into poor Mike

indicators.note: the second 'into' says the timber and the crash go inside the remaining letters
'poor' Mike is Mike in a bad state, so his letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: a log is a length of timber
to ram is to crash violently into something

explanation.surface: A heavy piece of wood is about to smash into an unlucky man called Mike.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'into' is the trick: the first belongs to the crash, while the second is the container signal, after the ellipsis.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilogramme is the metric base unit of mass, a standard measure of how heavy something is.

clue.text: (and 24) I may be only a theoretical construct, but to the social worker I'm of importance

definitions.text: I may be only a theoretical construct

parts.note: a worker ant is a member of a social insect colony, so the social worker is an ant
the speaker says they count for something: the first-person pronoun plus a verb meaning to be significant

explanation.surface: The speaker admits to being a mere idea in theory but says a social worker values them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' suggests a welfare professional; it is an ant. Read 'to the ant, I matter' and the halves join up.
explanation.definitionFit: Antimatter, made of antiparticles, was first predicted on paper by physicists before experiments found it.

clue.text: (and 19) The detective story is aromatically immaterial

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Umberto Eco's medieval murder mystery novel
second meaning: Juliet says a rose by any other name would smell as sweet, so what a rose is called makes no difference to its scent

explanation.surface: A book review grumbling that a crime novel has no smell worth mentioning.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense alludes to Romeo and Juliet: 'That which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet.'
explanation.definitionFit: Eco's novel is a whodunnit set in a monastery, and Shakespeare's line says a flower's label leaves its smell unchanged.

clue.text: Put away in a building on the street

indicators.note: in a down light one piece sits on another, so the street comes first and the rest follows

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street
taken as written
a shed is a simple outbuilding

explanation.surface: Goods are kept in a small outbuilding by the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the A and building after the street abbreviation, as in a down clue's stacking.
explanation.definitionFit: To stash something is to hide or store it away, so stashed means put away.
